comparison: Perfect agreement on findings beyond STG (C89, C92). Both evaluations support the identification of suppression in sensorimotor regions and isolated sites outside STG, with reviewers noting enhancement in frontal/motor areas and suppression in specific dorsal sensorimotor cortex and IFG regions.

Strong agreement on attentional interpretation (C11, C36-C37, C72, C79, C107, C111-C112, C114-C116). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct attentional controls, while peer reviewers SUPPORTED the interpretation. Both acknowledge the speculative nature but reviewers found the evidence convincing despite methodological limitations.

Strong agreement on anterior-posterior STG organization (C10, C35, C63, C65-C67, C70-C71, C78). Both evaluations SUPPORTED the finding that pSTG shows stronger DAF modulation than anterior STG. Reviewers acknowledged unusual effects but accepted the authors' control experiments. OpenEval emphasizes the TTS landmark and quantitative coordinates not explicitly mentioned in peer review.

Agreement on discrepancy with Chang et al. (C98-C103). Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN/speculative. OpenEval notes the explanations are appropriately acknowledged as speculative. Peer reviewers note methodological differences limit direct comparison and suggest the discrepancy should spawn additional research.

Strong agreement on correlation between suppression and sensitivity (C8, C33, C60-C62, C99, C104). Both SUPPORTED this core finding with reviewers praising the 'robust' analyses and 'convincing' evidence. Reviewers noted correlations are 'a little noisy' but positive, while OpenEval emphasizes the statistical significance (r=0.4006, p=0.002).

Agreement on common mechanism interpretation (C9, C34, C62). Both SUPPORTED this inference from the correlation data. OpenEval notes the cautious language appropriately reflects correlational evidence. Peer reviewers affirmed the finding addresses controversy 'in a rigorous fashion' regarding correlation between suppression and feedback sensitivity.

Strong agreement on topographical distribution and quantitative suppression data (C39-C47). Both SUPPORTED these findings. Peer reviewers praised 'greater dissection of the topography' and noted suppression is strongest in STG/MTG. OpenEval emphasizes the control experiment (VWR task, C49-C52) not explicitly mentioned in this peer result.

Agreement on topographical characterization (C6, C53-C54, C73, C80). Both SUPPORTED the findings on distribution and variability. Peer reviewers affirmed the topographical dissection without concerns. OpenEval emphasizes the lack of anatomical organization and high variability across sites.

Agreement on repetition suppression control (C49-C52). Both SUPPORTED this control analysis demonstrating speech-induced rather than repetition-based suppression. Peer reviewers noted controls were 'well done and clearly explained.' OpenEval emphasizes the strong correlation (r=0.9006) between AWR and VWR tasks.

Agreement on DAF effects and correlation with suppression (C7, C33, C57-C58, C74). Both SUPPORTED these findings. Peer reviewers noted the study demonstrates 'scaling of neural activity with degree of feedback delay' and found the correlation evidence 'convincing.' OpenEval emphasizes single-electrode examples and quantitative SensI ranges.

Agreement on behavioral and neural DAF effects from prior work (C55-C56). Both SUPPORTED these findings. Peer reviewers praised the 'robust' analyses including scaling with feedback delay degree. OpenEval notes these strengthen the current findings through citation of prior literature.

Agreement on voice intensity control (C64-C65). Both SUPPORTED this control analysis showing no difference between conditions. Peer reviewers accepted the controls for confounds without raising concerns. OpenEval emphasizes this control supports the anterior-posterior functional organization finding.

Agreement on study limitations (C105). Both acknowledge the lack of direct sensory controls. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED for appropriately identifying limitations. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted this limitation (UNCERTAIN) while noting unusual effects remain unclear despite control experiments.

OpenEval evaluated comprehensive methodological details (C5, C119-C128, C152-C154) covering participant recruitment, electrode specifications, recording equipment, and spatial coverage. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these methodological claims, though the editor confirmed 'appropriate experimental methods.'

OpenEval evaluated analytical methods in detail (C38, C48, C138-C171) including high gamma analysis, signal processing, SuppI/SensI calculations, and multitaper methods. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these analytical claims, though the editor confirmed 'appropriate...data, and analysis.'

OpenEval evaluated experimental procedures (C129-C147) including AWR, VWR, DAF, and VWR-AF task designs. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these procedural claims, though reviewers noted the work was 'well done and clearly explained.'

OpenEval evaluated background and motivation claims (C1-C25) establishing the literature context and knowledge gap. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these background claims, as peer reviews typically focus on novel findings rather than literature review.

OpenEval evaluated prior work on attention and speech monitoring (C28-C31, C108-C110). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these literature summary claims, though the attentional interpretation they support was evaluated by peer reviewers in R5.

OpenEval evaluated speculative hypothesis about division of labor (C82-C88) as UNCERTAIN, noting it is untested in the current study. No corresponding peer review evaluation addressed this speculative claim, likely because it was appropriately presented as future hypothesis rather than tested result.

OpenEval evaluated electrode localization methods (C148-C151, C155-C156) as SUPPORTED, noting standard and appropriate procedures. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these technical methodological claims.
